Cell 2 · markdown

Executive Summary

This project analyzes Airbnb listings in New York City to identify the key factors that influence nightly pricing. Airbnb hosts often struggle to determine competitive prices that maximize both occupancy and revenue, making data-driven pricing decisions essential in a highly competitive market. By examining listing characteristics such as location, room type, minimum stay requirements, host status, reviews, amenities, and availability, the project seeks to understand which variables have the greatest impact on listing performance.

The primary goal is to develop predictive models that help estimate listing prices while providing actionable recommendations for Airbnb hosts. The project aims to generate insights that improve pricing strategies, increase occupancy rates, and support better business decisions. The final outcome will be interpretable models and practical recommendations that enable hosts to optimize revenue and improve the overall performance of their listings.

Cell 3 · markdown

Business Understanding

Organization / Industry

Airbnb operates in the online hospitality and short-term rental industry, connecting property owners with travelers seeking temporary accommodations. Hosts compete in a dynamic marketplace where pricing, location, property features, and customer satisfaction significantly influence booking success. Because market conditions vary across neighborhoods and property types, hosts rely on accurate pricing strategies to remain competitive while maximizing occupancy and revenue.

Definition of the Business Challenge

The primary business challenge is determining which factors most strongly influence Airbnb listing prices in New York City. Hosts often lack sufficient insight into how variables such as location, room type, minimum stay requirements, reviews, amenities, host status, and availability affect listing performance. The project seeks to identify these key drivers and develop predictive models that support data-driven pricing decisions.

Business Impact and Importance

Accurate pricing is essential because it directly affects occupancy rates and revenue. Listings priced too high may experience fewer bookings, while listings priced too low reduce potential earnings. By identifying the characteristics that drive price, Airbnb hosts can optimize pricing strategies, improve occupancy, increase revenue, and strengthen their competitive position. The analysis also provides insights that can improve the overall efficiency and performance of Airbnb's marketplace.

Stakeholders Affected

  • Airbnb Hosts
  • Airbnb
  • Business Analysts
Cell 4 · markdown

Data Understanding

Source: Inside Airbnb – New York City

File Name: listings.csv, Inside Airbnb Data Dictionary - listings.csv detail v4.3

Description: Detailed Listings Data and Description of Columns

Website: https://insideairbnb.com/get-the-data/

The listings.csv dataset is a publicly available dataset published by Inside Airbnb that contains comprehensive information about Airbnb listings in New York City. It includes approximately 30,000 listings and 90 variables describing each property, including listing characteristics, host information, pricing, availability, reviews, and geographic location. The dataset is intended for research and data analysis and is compiled from publicly available information on Airbnb's website.

The Inside Airbnb Data Dictionary - listings.csv detail v4.3 shows the description of each column and what data is contained

import pandas as pd

    errors="coerce",
)

The distribution of listing prices is heavily right-skewed. Most Airbnb listings are priced below $300 per night, while a relatively small number of luxury listings create extreme price values. These outliers may influence predictive models and will be evaluated during preprocessing.

Cell 17 · markdown
Average listing prices vary considerably across New York City's boroughs. Manhattan has the highest average nightly price, followed by Brooklyn, while Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island have noticeably lower average prices. This indicates that location is a significant factor affecting Airbnb pricing.


Cell 18 · markdown
Data Quality Assessment


The exploratory analysis identified several data quality issues that may affect model performance. Approximately 8,700 listings have missing price values, which will require further investigation before model development. Several variables, including license, host_about, and bedrooms, contain substantial missing data. Some columns such as 'price_quote_price_per_night' have outliers that will need to be addressed before modeling. Additionally, some metadata fields related to host response information are largely incomplete and may not contribute meaningful predictive value.




Cell 19 · markdown
Data Preperation


Cell 20 · markdown
Missing Value Audit


The audit found substantial missingness in the listings dataset: 30,259 rows and 90 columns, with 28.9% of prices missing, twelve columns completely empty, and several key fields such as license, host_about, bedrooms, bathrooms, and beds missing at notable rates. The plan is to drop the target rows with missing price, remove the empty and non-predictive identifier/URL fields, treat structurally missing review data with indicators and sensible imputations, impute bedrooms/bathrooms/beds using room-type medians with missingness flags, and replace low-missingness categorical values with “Unknown,” while delaying all median calculations until after the train/test split to avoid leakage.


Cell 21 · code
Read Python source (177 lines)
import re
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


#Remove missing target values
df = df.loc[df["price"].notna()].copy()

# Remove implausible prices likely caused by data entry errors
rows_before = len(df)
df = df.loc[df["price"] >= 10].copy()
print(f"Implausible price rows removed (< $10): {rows_before - len(df):,}")

#Remove completely empty columns
all_missing_columns = df.columns[df.isna().all()].tolist()

    "review_scores_location",

]

for column in review_score_columns:
    if column in df.columns:
        df[f"{column}_missing"] = df[column].isna().astype("int8")

#Recover bathroom counts from bathrooms_text
def parse_bathroom_count(value):
    """
    Convert Airbnb bathroom text into a numeric count.

    Examples:
        "1 bath"              -> 1.0
        "1.5 shared baths"    -> 1.5
        "Private half-bath"   -> 0.5
        "Shared half-bath"    -> 0.5
    """
    if pd.isna(value):
        return np.nan

    text = str(value).strip().lower()

    if "half-bath" in text or "half bath" in text:
        number_match = re.search(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)?", text)
        return float(number_match.group()) if number_match else 0.5

    number_match = re.search(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)?", text)
    return float(number_match.group()) if number_match else np.nan


if "bathrooms_text" in df.columns and "bathrooms" in df.columns:
    parsed_bathrooms = df["bathrooms_text"].map(parse_bathroom_count)

    recovery_mask = df["bathrooms"].isna() & parsed_bathrooms.notna()
    df["bathrooms_recovered_from_text"] = recovery_mask.astype("int8")
    df.loc[recovery_mask, "bathrooms"] = parsed_bathrooms.loc[recovery_mask]

# A listing with zero reviews logically has no reviews-per-month history.
# Filling reviews_per_month with 0 is therefore a deterministic business rule,

if "number_of_reviews" in df.columns:

Cell 22 · markdown
Feature Engineering


This step engineers a cleaner modeling dataset by transforming skewed minimum-stay values, normalizing availability into comparable short-term and annual rates, grouping the many property types into broader categories, and adding a geographic distance feature from Midtown Manhattan. It will retain listing identifiers temporarily for validation and exclude them from the final model predictors. It will remove fields that should not be used as predictors, and it will avoid neighborhood average price for now because it could leak target information before the train/test split.

# Create Host Experience Features
def combine_years_and_months(year_column, month_column):
    """
    Convert separate year and month values into total months.

    If one component is present and the other is missing, the missing component
    is treated as zero. If both are missing, the result remains missing so a
    training-only imputer can handle it later.
    """
    years = pd.to_numeric(df[year_column], errors="coerce")
    months = pd.to_numeric(df[month_column], errors="coerce")

    both_missing = years.isna() & months.isna()
    total_months = years.fillna(0) * 12 + months.fillna(0)
    return total_months.mask(both_missing)


df["host_account_age_months"] = combine_years_and_months(
    "hosts_time_as_user_years",
    "hosts_time_as_user_months",
)

df["host_experience_months"] = combine_years_and_months(
    "hosts_time_as_host_years",
    "hosts_time_as_host_months",
)

host_tenure_components = [
    "hosts_time_as_user_years",
    "hosts_time_as_user_months",
    "hosts_time_as_host_years",
    "hosts_time_as_host_months",
]

df = df.drop(
    columns=[
        column for column in host_tenure_components if column in df.columns
    ]
)

import json
import ast

# Parse amenities and create stable tabular indicators
def parse_amenities(value):
    """
    Parse an Airbnb amenities list stored as JSON-like text.

    The function first attempts JSON parsing, then Python literal parsing, and
    finally uses a conservative comma split if the source text is malformed.
    """
    if pd.isna(value):
        return []

    if isinstance(value, list):
        return [str(item).strip() for item in value]

    text = str(value).strip()
    if not text:
        return []

    for parser in (json.loads, ast.literal_eval):
        try:
            parsed = parser(text)
            if isinstance(parsed, (list, tuple, set)):
                return [str(item).strip() for item in parsed]
        except (ValueError, TypeError, SyntaxError, json.JSONDecodeError):
            pass

    # Last-resort fallback for malformed rows.
    return [
        item.strip(" []\"'")
        for item in text.split(",")
        if item.strip(" []\"'")
    ]


amenity_lists = df["amenities"].map(parse_amenities)
amenity_text = amenity_lists.map(
    lambda items: " | ".join(item.lower() for item in items)
)

df["amenities_count"] = amenity_lists.map(len).astype("int16")

# Create binary amenity indicators
amenity_patterns = {
    "has_air_conditioning": (
        r"air conditioning|window ac|portable ac|central ac|"
        r"ac unit|split type ductless system"
    ),
    "has_kitchen": r"\bkitchen\b|kitchenette",
    "has_washer": r"\bwasher\b|washing machine",
    "has_dryer": r"\bdryer\b",
    "has_parking": r"parking|garage",
    "has_elevator": r"\belevator\b",
    "has_workspace": r"dedicated workspace|workspace|desk",
    "has_self_checkin": r"self check-in|self checkin",
    "allows_pets": r"pets allowed|pet-friendly|pet friendly",
    "has_gym": r"\bgym\b|exercise equipment|fitness",
    "has_pool": r"\bpool\b",
    "has_balcony_or_patio": r"balcony|patio",
}

for new_column, pattern in amenity_patterns.items():
    df[new_column] = (
        amenity_text
        .str.contains(
            pattern,
            case=False,
            na=False,
            regex=True
        )
        .astype("int8")
    )

df = df.drop(columns=["amenities"])

    df["last_scraped"],
    errors="coerce",

first_review_date = pd.to_datetime(
    df["first_review"],

    errors="coerce",
)

# Negative values are treated as data anomalies and clipped to zero.
days_since_last_review = (
    last_scraped_date - last_review_date
).dt.days.clip(lower=0)

review_history_days = (
    last_scraped_date - first_review_date
).dt.days.clip(lower=0)

has_reviews = pd.to_numeric(
    df["has_reviews"],
    errors="coerce",
).fillna(0).eq(1)

df["days_since_last_review"] = days_since_last_review.where(
    has_reviews,
    0,
)

df["review_history_days"] = review_history_days.where(
    has_reviews,
    0,
)

# Use at least 30 active days in the denominator to prevent division by zero or
# unstable annualized rates for a brand-new listing.
active_years = (
    (df["review_history_days"] + 1) / 365.25
).clip(lower=30 / 365.25)

number_of_reviews = pd.to_numeric(
    df["number_of_reviews"],
    errors="coerce",
).fillna(0)

df["reviews_per_active_year"] = (
    number_of_reviews / active_years
).where(has_reviews, 0)

# Remove raw review date fields after creating numeric review features
# Retain has_reviews and number_of_reviews as model predictors.
df = df.drop(
    columns=[
        "last_scraped",
        "first_review",
        "last_review",

# Group detailed property types into business categories
def group_property_type(value):
    """
    Map detailed Airbnb property descriptions into stable broad categories.

    The order matters. More specific categories such as serviced apartments and
    hotels are evaluated before broad categories such as houses.
    """
    if pd.isna(value):
        return "Other"

    text = str(value).strip().lower()

    if "serviced apartment" in text:
        return "Serviced apartment"

    if any(
        term in text
        for term in [
            "hotel",
            "aparthotel",
            "resort",
        ]
    ):
        return "Hotel"

    if any(
        term in text
        for term in [
            "hostel",
            "bed and breakfast",
            "dorm",
            "kezhan",
        ]
    ):
        return "Hostel or bed-and-breakfast"

    if any(term in text for term in ["guest suite", "guesthouse"]):
        return "Guest suite or guesthouse"

    if "rental unit" in text:
        return "Rental unit"

    if "condo" in text:
        return "Condo"

    if "townhouse" in text:
        return "Townhouse"

    if "loft" in text:
        return "Loft"

    if any(
        term in text
        for term in [
            "home",
            "house",
            "bungalow",
            "cottage",
            "villa",
            "vacation home",
        ]
    ):
        return "House"

    return "Other"


df["property_type_grouped"] = df["property_type"].map(
    group_property_type
).astype("string")

# Remove the detailed property type after grouping rare categories
df = df.drop(columns=["property_type"])

import math

# Create an approximate geographic-distance feature
# Fixed reference point: Times Square / Midtown Manhattan.
MIDTOWN_LATITUDE = 40.7580
MIDTOWN_LONGITUDE = -73.9855
EARTH_RADIUS_KM = 6371.0088

listing_latitude = pd.to_numeric(df["latitude"], errors="coerce")
listing_longitude = pd.to_numeric(df["longitude"], errors="coerce")

lat1 = np.radians(listing_latitude)
lon1 = np.radians(listing_longitude)
lat2 = math.radians(MIDTOWN_LATITUDE)
lon2 = math.radians(MIDTOWN_LONGITUDE)

delta_latitude = lat1 - lat2
delta_longitude = lon1 - lon2

haversine_a = (
    np.sin(delta_latitude / 2) ** 2
    + np.cos(lat1)
    * math.cos(lat2)
    * np.sin(delta_longitude / 2) ** 2
)

# Floating-point rounding can produce values just above 1.
haversine_a = np.clip(haversine_a, 0, 1)

df["distance_to_midtown_km"] = (
    2
    * EARTH_RADIUS_KM
    * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(haversine_a))
)

Predictor Selection and Train/Test Split


Both models will predict log_price. The original price is retained seperately so model predictions can later be converted back to dollars and evaluated with RMSE, MAE, and R-Squared. Split was intentionally done in this step so the data could be easily formatted for the two models.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Listing IDs are kept only for matching predictions back to listings.
# They are not included as model predictors.
listing_ids = df["id"].copy()

# Both models will be trained using the log-transformed target.
y_log = df["log_price"].astype(float)

# The original dollar price is retained for later model evaluation.
y_price = df["price"].astype(float)

# Define columns that should not be used as predictors

# Identifiers, names, scrape metadata, and descriptive text do not represent
# generalizable listing characteristics and could encourage memorization.
identifier_and_text_columns = [
    "id",
    "scrape_id",
    "source",
    "name",
    "host_id",
    "host_profile_id",
    "host_name",
    "host_location",
    "bathrooms_text",
    "calendar_last_scraped",
]

# These variables are excluded because engineered replacements already capture
# their useful information or because they are strongly redundant.
redundant_columns = [
    # host_portfolio_size replaces host_listings_count
    "host_listings_count",

    # Availability rates replace the raw availability counts
    "availability_30",
    "availability_365",
    "availability_eoy",

    # log_minimum_nights and minimum_stay_30_plus replace the raw and
    # highly redundant minimum-stay fields
    "minimum_nights",
    "minimum_minimum_nights",
    "maximum_minimum_nights",
    "minimum_nights_avg_ntm",

    # Retain maximum_nights as the primary maximum-stay variable
    "minimum_maximum_nights",
    "maximum_maximum_nights",
    "maximum_nights_avg_ntm",

    # reviews_per_active_year is the selected review-frequency measure
    "reviews_per_month",
]

# Neither target may appear in the predictor matrix.
target_columns = [
    "price",
    "log_price",
]

columns_to_exclude = (
    identifier_and_text_columns
    + redundant_columns
    + target_columns
)

# Drop only columns that exist so the code remains robust to small changes in
# the source file.
existing_columns_to_exclude = [
    column for column in columns_to_exclude
    if column in df.columns
]

X = df.drop(columns=existing_columns_to_exclude).copy()


# Create price strata for a balanced train/test split

# Nightly prices are strongly right-skewed. Dividing log_price into approximate
# deciles helps preserve a similar mix of low-, middle-, and high-price listings
# in the training and test datasets.
price_strata = pd.qcut(
    y_log,
    q=10,
    labels=False,
    duplicates="drop",
)


# Split predictors, targets, and IDs together

# The same 80/20 split is used for both models so their results can be compared
# fairly. random_state=42 makes the split reproducible.
(
    X_train,
    X_test,
    y_train_log,
    y_test_log,
    y_train_price,
    y_test_price,
    listing_ids_train,
    listing_ids_test,
) = train_test_split(
    X,
    y_log,
    y_price,
    listing_ids,
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=price_strata,
)



# Identify categorical and numeric predictor columns from training data

# Column types are determined after splitting. Phase 4 will use these lists to
# build leakage-safe imputing, encoding, and scaling pipelines.
categorical_columns = (
    X_train
    .select_dtypes(include=["object", "string", "category"])
    .columns
    .tolist()
)

numeric_columns = (
    X_train
    .select_dtypes(include=[np.number])
    .columns
    .tolist()
)



# Validation checks

# Confirm that target variables and identifiers are excluded from X.
assert "price" not in X.columns, (
    "Validation failed: price is present in the predictor matrix."
)

assert "log_price" not in X.columns, (
    "Validation failed: log_price is present in the predictor matrix."
)

for column in identifier_and_text_columns:
    assert column not in X.columns, (
        f"Validation failed: {column} should not be a predictor."
    )

# Confirm that the split did not lose or duplicate observations.
assert len(X_train) + len(X_test) == len(X), (
    "Validation failed: train and test row counts do not match X."
)

assert len(y_train_log) + len(y_test_log) == len(y_log), (
    "Validation failed: train and test target counts do not match y_log."
)

assert X_train.index.is_unique, (
    "Validation failed: duplicate indices exist in X_train."
)

assert X_test.index.is_unique, (
    "Validation failed: duplicate indices exist in X_test."
)

assert set(X_train.index).isdisjoint(set(X_test.index)), (
    "Validation failed: training and test indices overlap."
)

# Confirm that every predictor has been classified as numeric or categorical.
classified_columns = set(numeric_columns + categorical_columns)

assert classified_columns == set(X_train.columns), (
    "Validation failed: at least one predictor was not classified as "
    "numeric or categorical."
)

# Confirm that each aligned object has matching indices.
assert X_train.index.equals(y_train_log.index)
assert X_train.index.equals(y_train_price.index)
assert X_train.index.equals(listing_ids_train.index)

assert X_test.index.equals(y_test_log.index)
assert X_test.index.equals(y_test_price.index)
assert X_test.index.equals(listing_ids_test.index)



# Display Results

print("\nPhase 3 complete: Predictor selection and train/test split")

print(f"\nFull predictor matrix: {X.shape[0]:,} rows x {X.shape[1]:,} columns")
print(f"Training set: {X_train.shape[0]:,} rows x {X_train.shape[1]:,} columns")
print(f"Test set: {X_test.shape[0]:,} rows x {X_test.shape[1]:,} columns")

print(f"\nNumeric predictors: {len(numeric_columns)}")
print(f"Categorical predictors: {len(categorical_columns)}")

print("\nCategorical predictor columns:")
for column in categorical_columns:
    print(f"  - {column}")

print("\nTarget comparison:")
target_comparison = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Training log price": y_train_log.describe(),
        "Test log price": y_test_log.describe(),
        "Training dollar price": y_train_price.describe(),
        "Test dollar price": y_test_price.describe(),
    }
)

display(target_comparison.round(3))

print("\nMissing values remaining in the training predictors:")
training_missing = (
    X_train
    .isna()
    .sum()
    .loc[lambda values: values > 0]
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
)

display(
    training_missing
    .rename("Missing Training Values")

Missing-Value Imputation, Encoding, and Scaling


This phase creates two separate preprocessing pipelines:


    

  1. Linear Regression
    

      

    • Median imputation for numeric predictors
      • 

    • Standard scaling for numeric predictors
      • 

    • "Unknown" imputation for categorical predictors
      • 

    • One-hot encoding with one reference category dropped
      • 

    

    2. 

  2. Random Forest Regressor
    

      

    • Median imputation for numeric predictors
      • 

    • No numeric scaling
      • 

    • "Unknown" imputation for categorical predictors
      • 

    • One-hot encoding without dropping a category
      • 

    

    3. 



All preprocessing objects are fitted on X_train only. The fitted objects are
then used to transform X_test, preventing information from the test set from
leaking into model training.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from scipy import sparse
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler


# Create modeling copies of the Phase 3 train and test datasets
# The original X_train and X_test objects are preserved. These copies are used
# only for preprocessing and model development.
X_train_model = X_train.copy()
X_test_model = X_test.copy()


# Standardize missing-value representations
# Any positive or negative infinity values in numeric predictors are converted
# to NaN so the numeric imputer can handle them consistently.
X_train_model[numeric_columns] = (
    X_train_model[numeric_columns]
    .replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
)

X_test_model[numeric_columns] = (
    X_test_model[numeric_columns]
    .replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
)

# Convert categorical columns to object type and represent missing values as
# NumPy NaN. This gives SimpleImputer a consistent missing-value format.
for column in categorical_columns:
    X_train_model[column] = (
        X_train_model[column]
        .astype("object")
        .where(X_train_model[column].notna(), np.nan)
    )

    X_test_model[column] = (
        X_test_model[column]
        .astype("object")
        .where(X_test_model[column].notna(), np.nan)
    )


# 3. Confirm that no training predictor is completely missing
# A median or category cannot be learned from a column that is entirely missing.
all_missing_numeric_columns = [
    column
    for column in numeric_columns
    if X_train_model[column].isna().all()
]

all_missing_categorical_columns = [
    column
    for column in categorical_columns
    if X_train_model[column].isna().all()
]

if all_missing_numeric_columns:
    raise ValueError(
        "The following numeric training columns are completely missing: "
        f"{all_missing_numeric_columns}"
    )

if all_missing_categorical_columns:
    raise ValueError(
        "The following categorical training columns are completely missing: "
        f"{all_missing_categorical_columns}"
    )


# 4. Build the Linear Regression preprocessing pipeline
# Numeric predictors are imputed using training-set medians and standardized to
# a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1.
linear_numeric_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        (
            "imputer",
            SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
        ),
        (
            "scaler",
            StandardScaler()
        ),
    ]
)

# Categorical predictors are filled with "Unknown" and one-hot encoded.
# drop="first" creates a reference category for each categorical variable,
# reducing perfect multicollinearity in Linear Regression.
linear_categorical_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        (
            "imputer",
            SimpleImputer(
                strategy="constant",
                fill_value="Unknown"
            )
        ),
        (
            "onehot",
            OneHotEncoder(
                handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
                min_frequency=10,
                drop="first"
            )
        ),
    ]
)

linear_preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        (
            "numeric",
            linear_numeric_pipeline,
            numeric_columns
        ),
        (
            "categorical",
            linear_categorical_pipeline,
            categorical_columns
        ),
    ],
    remainder="drop"
)

# Build the Random Forest preprocessing pipeline
# Random Forest uses median imputation but does not require numeric scaling
# because decision trees split predictors using cutoff values.
rf_numeric_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        (
            "imputer",
            SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
        ),
    ]
)

# Random Forest keeps all one-hot categories because multicollinearity does not
# affect tree-based models in the same way it affects Linear Regression.
rf_categorical_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        (
            "imputer",
            SimpleImputer(
                strategy="constant",
                fill_value="Unknown"
            )
        ),
        (
            "onehot",
            OneHotEncoder(
                handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
                min_frequency=10
            )
        ),
    ]
)

rf_preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        (
            "numeric",
            rf_numeric_pipeline,
            numeric_columns
        ),
        (
            "categorical",
            rf_categorical_pipeline,
            categorical_columns
        ),
    ],
    remainder="drop"
)



# Fit preprocessing on training data and transform both datasets
# fit_transform learns medians, scaling statistics, and category levels from
# X_train_model only.
X_train_linear = linear_preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train_model)

# transform applies the already-fitted training transformations to the test set.
X_test_linear = linear_preprocessor.transform(X_test_model)

X_train_rf = rf_preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train_model)
X_test_rf = rf_preprocessor.transform(X_test_model)


# 7. Retrieve transformed feature names
# These names will be useful when interpreting Linear Regression coefficients
# and Random Forest feature importance values.
linear_feature_names = linear_preprocessor.get_feature_names_out()
rf_feature_names = rf_preprocessor.get_feature_names_out()



# 8. Validate the transformed datasets
def matrix_contains_invalid_values(matrix):
    """
    Return True when a dense or sparse matrix contains NaN or infinity.
    """
    if sparse.issparse(matrix):
        values = matrix.data
    else:
        values = np.asarray(matrix)

    return (
        np.isnan(values).any()
        or np.isinf(values).any()
    )


assert X_train_linear.shape[0] == X_train.shape[0], (
    "Validation failed: Linear Regression training row count changed."
)

assert X_test_linear.shape[0] == X_test.shape[0], (
    "Validation failed: Linear Regression test row count changed."
)

assert X_train_rf.shape[0] == X_train.shape[0], (
    "Validation failed: Random Forest training row count changed."
)

assert X_test_rf.shape[0] == X_test.shape[0], (
    "Validation failed: Random Forest test row count changed."
)

assert X_train_linear.shape[1] == len(linear_feature_names), (
    "Validation failed: Linear Regression feature-name count does not match "
    "the transformed matrix."
)

assert X_train_rf.shape[1] == len(rf_feature_names), (
    "Validation failed: Random Forest feature-name count does not match "
    "the transformed matrix."
)

assert not matrix_contains_invalid_values(X_train_linear), (
    "Validation failed: Linear Regression training data contains NaN or "
    "infinity after preprocessing."
)

assert not matrix_contains_invalid_values(X_test_linear), (
    "Validation failed: Linear Regression test data contains NaN or infinity "
    "after preprocessing."
)

assert not matrix_contains_invalid_values(X_train_rf), (
    "Validation failed: Random Forest training data contains NaN or infinity "
    "after preprocessing."
)

assert not matrix_contains_invalid_values(X_test_rf), (
    "Validation failed: Random Forest test data contains NaN or infinity "
    "after preprocessing."
)



# Display results

print("\nComplete: Imputation, encoding, and scaling")

print("\nLinear Regression preprocessing:")
print(
    f"  Training matrix: "
    f"{X_train_linear.shape[0]:,} rows x "
    f"{X_train_linear.shape[1]:,} transformed features"
)
print(
    f"  Test matrix: "
    f"{X_test_linear.shape[0]:,} rows x "
    f"{X_test_linear.shape[1]:,} transformed features"
)
print("  Numeric predictors: median-imputed and standardized")
print("  Categorical predictors: Unknown-imputed and one-hot encoded")
print("  First category dropped as the Linear Regression reference level")

print("\nRandom Forest preprocessing:")
print(
    f"  Training matrix: "
    f"{X_train_rf.shape[0]:,} rows x "
    f"{X_train_rf.shape[1]:,} transformed features"
)
print(
    f"  Test matrix: "
    f"{X_test_rf.shape[0]:,} rows x "
    f"{X_test_rf.shape[1]:,} transformed features"
)
print("  Numeric predictors: median-imputed without scaling")
print("  Categorical predictors: Unknown-imputed and one-hot encoded")
print("  All one-hot categories retained")

print("\nTraining-set missing values before preprocessing:")
print(f"  {int(X_train_model.isna().sum().sum()):,}")

print("\nInvalid values after preprocessing:")
print(
    "  Linear Regression training matrix: "
    f"{matrix_contains_invalid_values(X_train_linear)}"
)
print(
    "  Linear Regression test matrix: "
    f"{matrix_contains_invalid_values(X_test_linear)}"
)
print(
    "  Random Forest training matrix: "
    f"{matrix_contains_invalid_values(X_train_rf)}"
)
print(
    "  Random Forest test matrix: "
    f"{matrix_contains_invalid_values(X_test_rf)}"
)

print(
    "\nThe transformed matrices are ready for Linear Regression and "
    "Random Forest model training."
)

Cell 39 · markdown
Modeling


$Linear Regression$


Linear Regression will be used to predict Airbnb nightly prices by measuring the relationship between price and factors such as location, room type, amenities, reviews, and availability. This model is useful because it is easy to understand and shows how each variable affects the predicted price. It will help identify which features are associated with higher or lower listing prices. Since Airbnb prices are highly skewed, the model will predict the log-transformed price to reduce the influence of extreme outliers.

# =============================================================================
# Phase 5A: Linear Regression Model
# =============================================================================
# Paste this section directly after Phase 4.
#
# The model predicts log_price. Predictions are converted back to nightly
# prices in dollars for interpretation and evaluation.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Train the Linear Regression model
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
linear_model = LinearRegression()

linear_model.fit(
    X_train_linear,
    y_train_log
)

print("Linear Regression training complete.")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Generate predictions on the log-price scale
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
linear_train_predictions_log = linear_model.predict(X_train_linear)
linear_test_predictions_log = linear_model.predict(X_test_linear)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Convert predictions back to nightly prices in dollars
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# expm1 reverses the log1p transformation used on price.
# Negative predictions are set to zero because prices cannot be negative.
linear_train_predictions_price = np.maximum(
    np.expm1(linear_train_predictions_log),
    0
)

linear_test_predictions_price = np.maximum(
    np.expm1(linear_test_predictions_log),
    0
)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Evaluate Linear Regression
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def evaluate_linear_regression(
    actual_log,
    predicted_log,
    actual_price,
    predicted_price,
    dataset_name
):
    """
    Calculate RMSE, MAE, and R-squared on both the log and dollar scales.
    """
    return {
        "Model": "Linear Regression",
        "Dataset": dataset_name,
        "Log RMSE": np.sqrt(
            mean_squared_error(actual_log, predicted_log)
        ),
        "Log MAE": mean_absolute_error(
            actual_log,
            predicted_log
        ),
        "Log R-squared": r2_score(
            actual_log,
            predicted_log
        ),
        "Dollar RMSE": np.sqrt(
            mean_squared_error(actual_price, predicted_price)
        ),
        "Dollar MAE": mean_absolute_error(
            actual_price,
            predicted_price
        ),
        "Dollar R-squared": r2_score(
            actual_price,
            predicted_price
        ),
    }


linear_evaluation = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        evaluate_linear_regression(
            actual_log=y_train_log,
            predicted_log=linear_train_predictions_log,
            actual_price=y_train_price,
            predicted_price=linear_train_predictions_price,
            dataset_name="Training"
        ),
        evaluate_linear_regression(
            actual_log=y_test_log,
            predicted_log=linear_test_predictions_log,
            actual_price=y_test_price,
            predicted_price=linear_test_predictions_price,
            dataset_name="Test"
        ),
    ]
)

print("\nLinear Regression performance:")
display(linear_evaluation.round(4))


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Create listing-level prediction results
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
linear_prediction_results = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "listing_id": listing_ids_test,
        "actual_price": y_test_price,
        "linear_predicted_price": linear_test_predictions_price,
        "linear_absolute_error": np.abs(
            y_test_price.to_numpy()
            - linear_test_predictions_price
        ),
    },
    index=X_test.index
)

print("\nSample Linear Regression predictions:")
display(linear_prediction_results.head(10).round(2))


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Validate predictions
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
assert len(linear_test_predictions_price) == len(y_test_price), (
    "Validation failed: prediction count does not match the test target."
)

assert np.isfinite(linear_test_predictions_price).all(), (
    "Validation failed: Linear Regression produced a non-finite prediction."
)

assert (linear_test_predictions_price >= 0).all(), (
    "Validation failed: Linear Regression produced a negative price."
)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Plot actual versus predicted prices
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Limit the plot to the 99th percentile of actual prices so extreme luxury
# listings do not compress the majority of observations.
linear_plot_limit = float(y_test_price.quantile(0.99))

linear_plot_mask = (
    (y_test_price.to_numpy() <= linear_plot_limit)
    & (linear_test_predictions_price <= linear_plot_limit)
)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(
    y_test_price.to_numpy()[linear_plot_mask],
    linear_test_predictions_price[linear_plot_mask],
    alpha=0.35
)
plt.plot(
    [0, linear_plot_limit],
    [0, linear_plot_limit],
    linestyle="--"
)
plt.title("Linear Regression: Actual vs. Predicted Nightly Price")
plt.xlabel("Actual Price ($)")
plt.ylabel("Predicted Price ($)")
plt.xlim(0, linear_plot_limit)
plt.ylim(0, linear_plot_limit)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Plot residuals on the log-price scale
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
linear_residuals_log = (
    y_test_log.to_numpy()
    - linear_test_predictions_log
)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(
    linear_test_predictions_log,
    linear_residuals_log,
    alpha=0.35
)
plt.axhline(
    y=0,
    linestyle="--"
)
plt.title("Linear Regression Residual Plot")
plt.xlabel("Predicted Log Price")
plt.ylabel("Residual Log Price")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 9. Interpret Linear Regression coefficients
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Because the target is log_price:
# exp(coefficient) - 1 estimates the proportional price change associated with
# the feature, holding other predictors constant.
#
# Numeric predictors were standardized, so their coefficients represent an
# approximate one-standard-deviation change.
#
# Categorical coefficients compare each category with its dropped reference
# category.
linear_coefficients = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Feature": linear_feature_names,
        "Coefficient": linear_model.coef_,
    }
)

linear_coefficients["Absolute Coefficient"] = (
    linear_coefficients["Coefficient"].abs()
)

linear_coefficients["Estimated Percent Price Change"] = (
    np.expm1(linear_coefficients["Coefficient"]) * 100
)

linear_coefficients["Direction"] = np.where(
    linear_coefficients["Coefficient"] >= 0,
    "Higher predicted price",
    "Lower predicted price"
)

top_linear_coefficients = (
    linear_coefficients
    .sort_values(
        "Absolute Coefficient",
        ascending=False
    )
    .head(20)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

print("\nTop Linear Regression coefficients:")
display(top_linear_coefficients.round(4))


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 10. Plot the strongest Linear Regression coefficients
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
top_linear_for_plot = (
    top_linear_coefficients
    .sort_values("Absolute Coefficient")
)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
plt.barh(
    top_linear_for_plot["Feature"],
    top_linear_for_plot["Coefficient"]
)
plt.title("Top Linear Regression Coefficients")
plt.xlabel("Coefficient on Log Price")
plt.ylabel("Feature")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 11. Display test-set summary
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
linear_test_summary = (
    linear_evaluation
    .loc[linear_evaluation["Dataset"] == "Test"]
    .iloc[0]
)

print("\nLinear Regression test-set results:")
print(f"  RMSE: ${linear_test_summary['Dollar RMSE']:,.2f}")
print(f"  MAE: ${linear_test_summary['Dollar MAE']:,.2f}")
print(f"  R-squared: {linear_test_summary['Dollar R-squared']:.4f}")
Linear Regression training complete.

Linear Regression Results


The Linear Regression model performed poorly across the complete test set because a small number of extremely expensive listings created very large prediction errors. However, when the analysis was limited to listings below the 99th price percentile, or 1,483.20 per night, the model achieved an RMSE of 142.85, an MAE of 76.37, and an R² of 0.5801. These results indicate that the model explains approximately 58% of the variation in nightly prices for the majority of New York City Airbnb listings. The model is therefore more useful for typical listings than for extreme luxury properties.


Cell 47 · markdown
$Random Forest Regressor$


Random Forest Regressor will also be used to predict nightly Airbnb prices. It combines many decision trees and averages their predictions, which usually improves accuracy and reduces the chance of overfitting compared with using one decision tree. This model is useful because it can capture nonlinear relationships and interactions between variables that Linear Regression may miss. It can also show which features are most important when predicting listing prices. Model takes approx. 10 minutes to train


Cell 48 · code
Read Python source (274 lines)
# =============================================================================
# Phase 5B: Random Forest Regressor
# =============================================================================
# Paste this section directly after Phase 4.
#
# The model predicts log_price. Predictions are converted back to nightly
# prices in dollars for interpretation and evaluation.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Train the Random Forest Regressor
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# n_jobs=-1 uses all available CPU cores in Colab.
random_forest_model = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=300,
    max_depth=None,
    min_samples_split=5,
    min_samples_leaf=2,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

random_forest_model.fit(
    X_train_rf,
    y_train_log
)

print("Random Forest training complete.")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Generate predictions on the log-price scale
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
rf_train_predictions_log = random_forest_model.predict(X_train_rf)
rf_test_predictions_log = random_forest_model.predict(X_test_rf)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Convert predictions back to nightly prices in dollars
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# expm1 reverses the log1p transformation used on price.
# Negative predictions are set to zero because prices cannot be negative.
rf_train_predictions_price = np.maximum(
    np.expm1(rf_train_predictions_log),
    0
)

rf_test_predictions_price = np.maximum(
    np.expm1(rf_test_predictions_log),
    0
)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Evaluate the Random Forest model
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def evaluate_random_forest(
    actual_log,
    predicted_log,
    actual_price,
    predicted_price,
    dataset_name
):
    """
    Calculate RMSE, MAE, and R-squared on both the log and dollar scales.
    """
    return {
        "Model": "Random Forest",
        "Dataset": dataset_name,
        "Log RMSE": np.sqrt(
            mean_squared_error(actual_log, predicted_log)
        ),
        "Log MAE": mean_absolute_error(
            actual_log,
            predicted_log
        ),
        "Log R-squared": r2_score(
            actual_log,
            predicted_log
        ),
        "Dollar RMSE": np.sqrt(
            mean_squared_error(actual_price, predicted_price)
        ),
        "Dollar MAE": mean_absolute_error(
            actual_price,
            predicted_price
        ),
        "Dollar R-squared": r2_score(
            actual_price,
            predicted_price
        ),
    }


random_forest_evaluation = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        evaluate_random_forest(
            actual_log=y_train_log,
            predicted_log=rf_train_predictions_log,
            actual_price=y_train_price,
            predicted_price=rf_train_predictions_price,
            dataset_name="Training"
        ),
        evaluate_random_forest(
            actual_log=y_test_log,
            predicted_log=rf_test_predictions_log,
            actual_price=y_test_price,
            predicted_price=rf_test_predictions_price,
            dataset_name="Test"
        ),
    ]
)

print("\nRandom Forest performance:")
display(random_forest_evaluation.round(4))


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Create listing-level prediction results
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
random_forest_prediction_results = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "listing_id": listing_ids_test,
        "actual_price": y_test_price,
        "random_forest_predicted_price": rf_test_predictions_price,
        "random_forest_absolute_error": np.abs(
            y_test_price.to_numpy()
            - rf_test_predictions_price
        ),
    },
    index=X_test.index
)

print("\nSample Random Forest predictions:")
display(random_forest_prediction_results.head(10).round(2))


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Validate predictions
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
assert len(rf_test_predictions_price) == len(y_test_price), (
    "Validation failed: prediction count does not match the test target."
)

assert np.isfinite(rf_test_predictions_price).all(), (
    "Validation failed: Random Forest produced a non-finite prediction."
)

assert (rf_test_predictions_price >= 0).all(), (
    "Validation failed: Random Forest produced a negative price."
)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Plot actual versus predicted prices
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Limit the plot to the 99th percentile of actual prices so extreme luxury
# listings do not compress the majority of observations.
rf_plot_limit = float(y_test_price.quantile(0.99))

rf_plot_mask = (
    (y_test_price.to_numpy() <= rf_plot_limit)
    & (rf_test_predictions_price <= rf_plot_limit)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(
    y_test_price.to_numpy()[rf_plot_mask],
    rf_test_predictions_price[rf_plot_mask],
    alpha=0.35
)
plt.plot(
    [0, rf_plot_limit],
    [0, rf_plot_limit],
    linestyle="--"

plt.title("Random Forest: Actual vs. Predicted Nightly Price")
plt.xlabel("Actual Price ($)")
plt.ylabel("Predicted Price ($)")
plt.xlim(0, rf_plot_limit)
plt.ylim(0, rf_plot_limit)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Plot residuals on the log-price scale

    y_test_log.to_numpy()
    - rf_test_predictions_log

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))

Random Forest Tuning


The training set used on the Random Forest will now be tuned using RandomizedSearchCV with a 2-fold cross validation. This will take 5 minutes to validate.


Cell 53 · code
Read Python source (88 lines)
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Create a search sample
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tuning on a 5,000-row sample keeps the search computationally practical.
# The best configuration is then retrained on the full training set.
rng = np.random.RandomState(42)

sample_size = min(5_000, X_train_rf.shape[0])
sample_indices = rng.choice(
    X_train_rf.shape[0],
    size=sample_size,
    replace=False,
)

X_search = X_train_rf[sample_indices]
y_search = y_train_log.to_numpy()[sample_indices]

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Run the randomized search
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Parallelism is applied only at the search level to avoid CPU contention.
rf_param_distributions = {
    "max_depth": [None, 20, 30],
    "min_samples_split": [2, 5, 10],
    "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 4],
    "max_features": ["sqrt", 0.3],
}

rf_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=100,
        random_state=42,
        n_jobs=1,
    ),
    param_distributions=rf_param_distributions,
    n_iter=5,
    cv=2,
    scoring="neg_mean_squared_error",
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=2,
)

rf_search.fit(X_search, y_search)

print("Best parameters found:")
print(rf_search.best_params_)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Retrain the best configuration on the full training set
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
tuned_rf_model = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=200,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1,
    **rf_search.best_params_,
)

tuned_rf_model.fit(X_train_rf, y_train_log)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Evaluate the tuned model on the test set
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
tuned_rf_test_predictions_log = tuned_rf_model.predict(X_test_rf)

tuned_rf_test_predictions_price = np.maximum(
    np.expm1(tuned_rf_test_predictions_log),
    0
)

tuned_rf_rmse = np.sqrt(
    mean_squared_error(y_test_price, tuned_rf_test_predictions_price)
)

tuned_rf_mae = mean_absolute_error(
    y_test_price, tuned_rf_test_predictions_price
)

tuned_rf_r2 = r2_score(
    y_test_price, tuned_rf_test_predictions_price
)

print("\nTuned Random Forest test-set results:")
print(f"RMSE: ${tuned_rf_rmse:,.2f}")
print(f"MAE: ${tuned_rf_mae:,.2f}")
print(f"R-squared: {tuned_rf_r2:.4f}")

if not csv_files:

# Prefer a file specifically named listings.csv.
# Otherwise, use the largest uploaded CSV.
filename = next(
    (
        name for name in csv_files
        if name.lower() == "listings.csv"
    ),
    max(
        csv_files,
        key=lambda name: len(uploaded[name])
    )
)

df = pd.read_csv(

)

Cell 58 · markdown
Evaluation Summary


All the models were evaluated using the same test set using RMSE, MAE, and R-Ssquared.


Results


The Mean-Price Baseline by MAE was $194. Linear Regression reduced MAE to $122 but it has a -9.97 R-Squared which means that it fails on luxury listings. When it was restricted to below the 99th percentile, it performed far better.


The Random Forest model was the best performing model. On the full test set it had an RMSE of $282, and MAE of $78 and R-Squared of .54. Below the 99th percentile, it has a price limit of $1,483.20, RMSE of $124.22, MAE of $61.81, and R-squared of 0.6825. It outperforms the Linear Regression model across every metric. Even on the trimmed set and the Hyperparemeter tuning it performed well.


Business Interpretation


If using the Randon Forest model, businesses can be able to estimate what the average listing would be for a nightly price. It is more accurate than hosts guessing prices that are competative and then not getting any bookings. Using a Regression Model wouldn't be able to give you these accurate estimations and predictions.


Limitations and Risks


One of the biggest limitation is that the models aren't good at predicting luxury listings reliably. So if you are an owner of a place that goes for $1,400 per night or more, the model will have a hard time to predict the rest of the market.


The data used is also based on a location and only that. It doesn't take into account high and low seasons where you can charge more or less depending on the time of year, it also doesn't account for holidays or events happening. This can be beneficial for hosts so that they can adjust their prices based on events or special activites happening where it is justified to increase prices.


Cell 59 · markdown
Conclusions and Recommendations


Best Performing Model


The Random Forest Regressor is the recommended model since it outperformed both the mean-price baseline and the Linear Regression across every metric on the full test set. Random Forest Regressor explains around 54% of the variation in nightly prices with an average absolute error of $79 per night. It does well at knowing the price structure of all listing across New York City. Linear Regression can be used to help indentify how individual features in the listing can affect the price of the stay but it shouldn't be used as the method to price the listing.


Recommendations


Use the Random Forest Regressor model to get rough prices for listings. As long as it is under $1,400 per night, the model can use market data to help you competitively price your place.


Make sure that listings under $1,400 are being used in the model. If you have a place above $1,400 per night, do not use the model as it will be innacurate.


Cell 60 · markdown
Ethical Considerations


This project raises several important ethical considerations. One concern is bias in the dataset, as the historical data may not accurately represent all customer groups. If certain groups are underrepresented or overrepresented, the model's predictions may unfairly favor or disadvantage those customers. During the cleaning process, we removed 8,744 rows with missing prices which may also introduce a selection bias.


Another concern is privacy. Customer data should be collected, stored, and analyzed securely to protect sensitive personal information. Organizations should comply with privacy laws and ensure that customer data is only used for legitimate business purposes.


There is also a risk of misusing predictive analytics. If the model incorrectly predicts that a customer will not respond, the business could miss potential sales opportunities. Likewise, inaccurate predictions could result in customers receiving unnecessary marketing calls, negatively affecting their experience.


To promote fairness and transparency, businesses should regularly evaluate their models for bias, explain how predictions are made, and avoid relying solely on automated decision-making. Human oversight should be used when making important business decisions.


When used responsibly, predictive analytics can help businesses improve efficiency, reduce costs, and better target customers. However, organizations must recognize the limitations of the model and use its predictions as decision-support tools rather than replacing human judgment.
